rationale: The student added both the numerators and the denominators (2/5 + 1/5 = 3/10). A number line divided into equal fifths demonstrates that adding unit fractions increments the count of fifths while the unit size (denominator) remains unchanged.

script.focus: the tick label showing that the denominator stays 5

intent: Demonstrate add on the number-line with values [1,3] (unit 1/5). Tutor points at: the tick label showing that the denominator stays 5

frames.caption: Start at 1/5. We are standing here; we have not hopped yet.
Hop 1 moves 1/5 forward and lands on 2/5. One hop is one fifth.
Hop 3 lands on 4/5. 3 hops, so 1/5 + 3/5 = 4/5. Every hop was one fifth; the size of the pieces never changed, only how many.

judgement.reasoning: The student incorrectly added denominators (2/5 + 1/5 = 3/10). The detour uses a number line demonstration showing hops of 1/5, clearly emphasizing that the step size remains fifths and that 1/5 + 3/5 = 4/5. A number line provides an effective alternate representation to the fraction bar, directly illustrating why the denominator remains unchanged.
judgement.verdict: Yes, a teacher would definitely use this clear number-line demonstration to visually show why the denominator stays fifths during addition.
